Rethinking this, we should probably make sup tags obligatory.
* If each dup and sup is given an unique label, the user-provided sups will never be annihilated.
* If dup and sup labels can overlap and are generated independently, we get behaviour that depends on other functions and that the user has no control. Depending on arbitrary decisions of the compiler, a sup may interact with dups that have equal or different labels, leading to different results.

So, to me the only sensible option is to force sups to have explicit labels

Three problems with the probe here:

1. **Wrong timing.** It runs inside the loop that also calls each due waiter's `a->pack`. An earlier callback (say, a timed-out `try_accept` that still calls `accept()`) can take the lowest free number before a later waiter on that closed number is probed. The probe then sees a valid fd, and the waiter stays parked on someone else's connection. The JS version checks every waiter before any callback runs; C should do the same.
2. **Wrong test.** `F_GETFD` isn't what `select` checks. A zero-timeout `poll()` on each parked fd, looking for `POLLNVAL`, checks the same thing `select` does. That makes the recovery exact, and combined with the fatal fallback above, it removes the spin.
3. **Helper-thread race.** `io_help` threads open files (`File.open`) concurrently, so a closed number can be reused between the `EBADF` and the probe. No probe can detect a number that is reused before `select` runs. We can still keep the window minimal by probing right after `select`, before anything else.

Minor: `pnd` is always the first call's held-word count, but the nested ternaries recompute it on every iteration. Computing it once after the first call would make the `STK(${pnd - depth})` offsets much easier to check.

Removing the `if (FL.js) return;` guard lets JS reach the C-only `u64 … = heap_alloc` hoist. JS output is only safe because this regex happens not to match any JS today. A JS arm starting with `u64 x = heap_alloc(e, N);` (from an intrinsic/foreign template or a future emitter change) would be hoisted into invalid JS. Every multi-arm JS chain also now joins its lines and runs the regex, and nested chains repeat that at each level, just to get the `undefined` the guard returned for free.

`ty_adt(ty)` (an unmemoized `ty_wnf` → `Bend.term_wnf`) now runs once per table cell instead of once per table. In JS, a lookup table with hundreds of rows does hundreds of identical whnf reductions. Suggest hoisting `const k = ty_adt(ty)!.k` back out.

`[...tag, ...fs.flatMap((f) => f.ws)]` is rebuilt inside the `lay.ks.map` callback, once per layout word. That makes each constructor site O(W²) on the C hot path, and wide records near `WIDE` pay it at every construction. The old `ws` local was the cheap form.

`ctr_live(FL.book.ctrs[x.k])` now runs once per field, and each call does a `ctr_tail` (tele_unbind lookup + slice) plus `filter(dom_live)`. That's O(n²) per constructor expression in JS output. Suggest restoring the `fs` local.

`ctr_flds(s.k, s.x)` (`ctr_tail` + a filter over every field) is called inside the per-field map, followed by an O(n) `includes`. `anf` walks every def body, so this makes every `Ctr` node O(n²) instead of O(n). Suggest hoisting it.

`let_live(s)` isn't memoized (it does a term_open lookup plus `rest_use` for every binder), and it's now called inside the per-binding loop. A Let with n binders recomputes all n liveness flags n times just to read one entry each time. `let_live` stays hoisted elsewhere in this PR for exactly this reason.

The `t.$ === "Mat" ? Math.max : (a, b) => a + b` ternary is now evaluated inside the reduce callback, so a fresh adder closure is allocated per child instead of per node. `term_uses` runs on every subterm of every compiled def, so this is extra GC pressure on one of the hottest walks.
`lays.flatMap((m) => m.ks).length` is recomputed for every multi-word lay (O(L·K) instead of once). It's minor since `fun_of` is memoized per def, but the old `wide` local was also clearer.

`reach` rebuilds the full edge list (`all.flatMap` over every seg's refs) on each call, and it's called twice (`live` and `dev`). That's an extra full allocation on every C compile, to save one identifier.

`push_macro` saves an include guard's earlier state but never `#undef`s it. If the guard is already defined, the HID copy skips its own guarded body.

Example: a program imports bend-kit-time v1 (no HID, `#ifndef TIME_EFFS` guard) and v2 (HID, same guard, since the guide says guards don't need HID). v1 is in the non-HID part, so it's pasted first and defines `TIME_EFFS`. v2's copy then skips its own helpers and fails with an undeclared `HID_..._helper`. If the guarded block only has macros, v2 silently uses v1's, which is #1533 again. Emitting `#undef NAME` after each `push_macro` fixes it.

This skips HID enforcement when the root module imports the package's C (`m === ""`). So the author's own build never catches a bare name, contrary to the PR's claim. A package author who runs `bend -o out lib.bend` on the file that does `import "./lib.c"` (like `effect_version_a.bend`) gets no dead copy, and a bare `static int count;` passes. The clash only shows up when a user imports two versions.

`HID(k)` always resolves in the importing module's namespace, so a package's C can't name Base's effect internals, which are now HID-renamed, or another package's.

A hub package whose C extends windows or channels by naming Base's `BendWin`, `WinQueue` or a chan.c helper breaks after the Base conversion. The bare name is undeclared, and `HID(BendWin)` in the package gives `HID_pkg_BendWin`, not Base's `HID__BendWin`. Only the root file (namespace `""`) can reach Base, so there's no supported way to depend on another module's C.

The dead copy only neutralizes constructor and destructor attributes. Objective-C in it still runs or registers at image load: `+load` methods run and categories attach.

Example: a macOS package with an `#ifdef __OBJC__` path defines `@implementation NSWindow (HID(Ext))` or a class with `+load`. The dead copy's `+load` runs at startup a second time. Its category methods share copy 1's selectors and may win, and they read `HID2_` globals whose constructor never ran.

The dead copy keeps every external-linkage function and the data it reaches, so a package's initialized tables end up twice in every consuming binary. For example, a non-static `Term HID(run)(...)` that reads a 2 MB `static const u8 HID(font)[]` gets a second, unused 2 MB `HID2_` copy, and -O3 can't drop it because the `HID2_` entry point has external linkage. The 136-byte cost in the PR description only holds for tiny packages.

Non-HID effect sources are still joined with `""` (the HID path uses `"\n"`), so a `.c` file without a trailing newline merges into the next one. `#endif` followed by `Term foo(...)` becomes `#endifTerm foo(...)`, an invalid directive. If the first file ends in a `//` comment, the next file's first line becomes part of the comment.

**Design:** this enforces an author-side lint by compiling every HID package's C twice in every downstream build. That costs compile time and binary size, needs clang 21, and still misses Base and root. It also brings the issues above: ObjC load side effects, no constructor priorities, and false tentative-definition errors. All to catch a mistake only the publisher can fix.

The same check, run once when a package is tested or published on the hub, or as a TS-side scan of top-level definitions, would enforce the rule with no per-build cost.

`at()` reruns the `#define`/`#undef` regex over the whole module source and re-splits `dead` on each of its four calls per module. Computing `const names = [...dead, ...macros]` once per module and mapping it to push and pop avoids that. Making `dead` an array also removes the split and the `replace`.
